title: How Lawmakers Fund Each Other
hook: Some of the most important campaign money in Congress doesn't come from voters or donors — it flows between lawmakers themselves, and it quietly buys power.
key_points: Members of Congress legally transfer campaign funds to colleagues, often through 'leadership PACs,' to build support and steer money to tight races.
Party leaders are the biggest givers: researchers found a large majority of leaders donate to colleagues, far more than rank-and-file members do.
When an outside super PAC attacks a vulnerable member, fellow partisans respond by sending that colleague more money.
These internal flows let leaders reward loyalty, protect at-risk seats, and shape who rises in the party.
The lesson: campaign finance isn't only donors-to-candidates — power is also organized inside the party, member to member.
content_html: Ask where a member of Congress's campaign money comes from and you'll picture donors and small-dollar givers. But a quieter, strategically vital stream runs sideways — from one lawmaker to another — and following it explains a lot about who holds power inside a party.
extra_html: In The Conversation, researcher Mayank Kejriwal describes how House members routinely route campaign money to their colleagues, frequently through "leadership PACs," in transfers that are legal and publicly reported. His analysis finds that party leaders dominate the giving: a far larger share of formal leaders contribute to colleagues than rank-and-file members do. The money is strategic — when an outside super PAC targets a vulnerable incumbent, fellow partisans respond by boosting their contributions to that endangered colleague, signaling the race matters and rallying internal support. Over time these flows let leaders reward loyalty, protect at-risk seats, and influence who climbs the ranks. The broader lesson is that campaign finance isn't only a story of outside donors and candidates; a great deal of power is organized inside the party itself, member to member. (U.S. Congress example.)

related.title: Political Parties & Party Systems
related.hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

related.title: Political Corruption
related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

flashcards.back_html: A political action committee a lawmaker uses to raise money and donate it to colleagues — building support and influence within their party.

flashcards.prompt: What did the research find about who gives the most money to fellow House members?

choices.text: Party leaders give at much higher rates than rank-and-file members
Rank-and-file members give far more than leaders
Members almost never give money to one another

flashcards.explanation_html: A large majority of formal leaders contributed to colleagues, well above non-leaders — concentrating influence at the top of the party.

flashcards.prompt: How do fellow partisans typically react when a super PAC targets a vulnerable member?

choices.text: They increase their own contributions to the endangered colleague
They withdraw support to avoid the controversy
They redirect their donations to the attacking PAC

flashcards.explanation_html: Internal giving rises to protect at-risk members, signaling the race is strategically important to the party.
